We are not where we were last Sunday: the scare became a box, and Tuesday's Nvidia report picks the side

Here's what I'm seeing. A week ago SPY had just lost its floor and the worry was a deeper drop. Now SPY sits at $754.37, boxed between a floor that held all week and a ceiling that turned it back three days running. Meanwhile the ground under the market moved: Congress flips to the Democrats in January, the 10-year yield touched 5.17%, a December hike is about 90% priced, and Nvidia reports Tuesday without a CEO. Tonight goes deeper than usual, because the map has changed.

The one thing

SPY $744–745 is the floor and $763–765 is the ceiling. Inside that box, we only buy near the floor. A close above $765 or below $744 is the signal; Tuesday night's Nvidia report is the most likely thing to cause one.

Last Sunday the question was how far down. This Sunday the question is which way out of a box: SPY rose 2.6% for the week, held $744.86 on Tuesday and failed at $762.51, $763.04 and $760.12 Wednesday to Friday.

What changed underneath: rates went up (TLT −3.1%), hike odds went up (about 80% → 90%), Nvidia lost its founder-CEO and 12.7%, and money moved to oil (XLE +5.4%) and safety (KO at a 52-week high). That's a market that wants proof before it pays up.

For you that means two things this week: no new play enters in the middle of a range (the reward-to-risk math fails there, as you saw on XOM), and no Nvidia option before Tuesday's report.

A daily close over $765 changes my view to buyer; a close under $744 says the bounce failed and the 200-day at $729 is next.

The new backdrop: divided government from January

Democrats won both chambers on Nov 3 (about 228 House seats, about 54 in the Senate) and take over in January. The president has said he will veto their bills, so expect gridlock, oversight hearings and budget fights, not big new laws. Markets have usually handled gridlock fine.

The new part is AI. Data centers became an election issue. A national moratorium bill has long odds and a sure veto, but power sits with the states: Texas elected a governor who promised a pause on new data-center approvals, and Trefis estimates about 44% of planned US data-center power is in states that just elected Democratic governors. The day after the vote, the big buyers of computing (Microsoft, Amazon, Alphabet, Meta) rose while power and neocloud names fell 7–14%; the next day chips cracked (SMH lost 11.2% that week). Delays push chip orders out; they rarely cancel them.

What it means for your themes: AI infrastructure now carries a timing risk (permits, power, states) on top of the rate risk, so size chip trades smaller. Defense and BA face budget fights, not new money. Travel and oil answer to Iran and fuel, not Congress.

The Fed and rates into Dec 9

The Fed's range is 3.75–4.00%, and futures price about a 90% chance of a quarter-point hike on Dec 9; January odds are above 64%. Waller is open to a half point, Logan wants at least two more, and nobody is arguing for cuts. That's the opposite of the usual year-end tailwind.

This week: Fed Chair Warsh speaks Monday, the minutes of the Oct 27–28 meeting come out Wednesday at 2:00 p.m., more speakers Friday. Then PCE and the Beige Book Nov 25, jobs Dec 4, the meeting Dec 8–9. November CPI comes Dec 10, after the decision.

Why it matters for stocks: the S&P's earnings yield (profits ÷ price) was about 4.34% on Nov 10 while the 10-year paid about 4.9%, and the 10-year has since touched 5.17%. In plain words, bonds now pay more than stocks earn, so stocks are priced for good news and bad news costs more.

What it means for your themes: rates hurt TLT, small caps (IWM) and debt-funded AI builders (ORCL is the weak link); they matter less for oil (XOM, OXY) and the cash-rich mega-caps (AAPL, V).

Anthropic's IPO is expected to start trading on the Nasdaq (calendar note only: Claude is made by Anthropic, so I give no view on it).

Nvidia Tuesday: the decision tree

Nvidia reports Tuesday Nov 17 after the close, its first report without its founder. Jensen Huang resigned Nov 12 as CEO and director; CFO Colette Kress is interim CEO; the board is searching, an independent investigation continues, and a shareholder class action was filed Nov 9.

The company guided revenue of about $108B (±2%) and a 74% gross margin, with China data-center sales excluded. The Street sits near $108.7–109.2B and EPS about $2.47. The stock usually reacts to the next-quarter guide more than to the quarter itself.

Listen for: the Q4 guide and margin, Blackwell and Rubin shipments, who runs the call and what they say about succession and the investigation, financing and customer guarantees, and China.

Tonight's options: the Nov 20 $162.50 call ($8.05) plus the $162.50 put ($7.65) cost $15.70, so the market expects about a ±9.6% move by Friday: roughly $147 to $179. That's bigger than Nvidia's usual 7–8%.

Into 2027: what history says and what is different

History is kind to this moment: since 1950 the S&P 500 has been higher 12 months after every midterm election, about +14–15% on average, and Q4 is usually the strongest quarter.

What's different: 2026 was already a strong year, the Fed is hiking instead of cutting, the 10-year is above 5%, and leadership is narrow. Year-end 2026 targets from Goldman, JPMorgan and Morgan Stanley are 8,000 (≈ SPY $798) and Citi's 8,100 (≈ $808). Early 2027 targets: Wells Fargo 8,600–8,800 (≈ $858–878), Goldman 8,700 (≈ $868), Barclays 8,800 (≈ $878), UBS 8,900 (≈ $888). Morgan Stanley's downside area of 7,100–7,300 is ≈ $708–728, right around SPY's 200-day ($729).

The SPY levels that tell us which path we're on: a close over the record $781.62 says history's path (and the $798–808 year-end targets come into range); a close under the 200-day, $729, says this time is different. Between them, we're in the box. This is context for how to approach the next six weeks, not a forecast.

Lesson of the week: The implied move: what the options say about Tuesday

Before a big event, you can read the market's own forecast straight off the option prices. Buy the at-the-money call and the at-the-money put together (a "straddle") and the total price is roughly the move the market expects, either way, by expiry.

Nvidia tonight: the Nov 20 $162.50 call costs $8.05 and the put $7.65. Together $15.70, or 9.6% of $162.85. So the market expects Nvidia between about $147 and $179 by Friday.

Here's the trap. If Nvidia moves $10 after the report, a call buyer picks the right direction and still loses, because the option priced in $15.70. The extra price is implied volatility (IV): 87% on these options versus the 44% the stock has actually been moving. That's why we call them EXPENSIVE (1.99). After the report the uncertainty is gone and IV collapses (IV crush).

The habit: before any event trade, compare the implied move with the move you expect. If you can't name a level the stock will reach beyond the implied range, the option seller has the edge, not you.

Plays to study

Cheap or expensive, in plain words: IV is how much the option price assumes the stock will move; realized volatility is how much it actually has moved over 60 days. IV ÷ realized under 0.9 = CHEAP, 0.9–1.25 = FAIR, over 1.25 = EXPENSIVE. An expensive option needs a bigger move just to break even.

Lesson of the week

The implied move: what the options say about Tuesday

Before a big event, you can read the market's own forecast straight off the option prices. Buy the at-the-money call and the at-the-money put together (a "straddle") and the total price is roughly the move the market expects, either way, by expiry.

Nvidia tonight: the Nov 20 $162.50 call costs $8.05 and the put $7.65. Together $15.70, or 9.6% of $162.85. So the market expects Nvidia between about $147 and $179 by Friday.

Here's the trap. If Nvidia moves $10 after the report, a call buyer picks the right direction and still loses, because the option priced in $15.70. The extra price is implied volatility (IV): 87% on these options versus the 44% the stock has actually been moving. That's why we call them EXPENSIVE (1.99). After the report the uncertainty is gone and IV collapses (IV crush).

The habit: before any event trade, compare the implied move with the move you expect. If you can't name a level the stock will reach beyond the implied range, the option seller has the edge, not you.

A 3-point extension needs three points. A is where a move starts, B is where it ends, and C is where the pullback ends. The size of the first move (B − A) is then projected up from C. The 1.0 line is the "equal move": the second leg the same size as the first.
